additions.text: He is one who has obtained the gain that is his own true nature. For the person who seeks liberation, the yogins declare association with women to be a gateway to hell.
Māyā in the form of a woman approaches gradually under the pretext of service and similar acts. One should regard that māyā as death, hostile to one’s purpose.

He states the same teaching for a woman who seeks liberation in two verses beginning with “whom she considers.” A woman may regard My māyā, acting in the form of a man and appearing as a husband who gives wealth and the like, as her protector; she should know that male-form māyā as death. The reason is that a living being who in a former birth was male, through attachment to a woman and meditation upon her at death, may attain womanhood. Thus she should recognize the husband and similar male forms as death. The comparison is with the hunter’s song: although it appears agreeable to a deer, it leads to the deer’s death.

Thus the transmigration of the living being has been elaborated, including travel from world to world under karma and birth and death. A doubt arises: how can an all-pervading living being travel from one world to another, and how can one that is eternal be born and die? If karma is exhausted by experience, why should birth and death recur, and from where would further karma arise? He answers that the living being travels to another world together with the subtle body that has arisen as a limiting adjunct. By continuously performing actions, the stream of karma is never brought to an end.

He explains how birth and death are possible. The subtle body, the limiting adjunct called the jīva-body, follows this self. The gross body, made of the elements, senses, and mind, is the field of experience. When these two become incapable of functioning, that cessation is called the living being’s death; their manifestation and coming into operation is called birth.

He makes this clear with an illustration. When the physical locus of perception, such as the eyeball, becomes incapable of seeing an object because of cataract or another defect, the eye-sense also becomes incapable. When both the bodily locus and the eye-sense are incapable, the seer, the jīva, is incapable of exercising sight. In the same way, impairment of the gross body brings impairment of the subtle body; that is called the living being’s death, not a destruction of the living being itself. Some recensions read an additional verse here. On that reading, the inability of the gross body, the locus for apprehending objects, is called its dissolution or death, while the manifestation of the gross body through the egoistic cognition “this is I” is its birth; inability of the eye-globes to reveal the object’s form is explained similarly. The remainder is the same. Since in reality the living being itself does not undergo birth and death, one should not be terrified of death, nor should one become abject about remaining alive, nor agitated in one’s efforts to preserve life.

An objection is raised: if one is entirely free from attachment, how can one continue living? He answers that with rightly seeing intelligence one should place the body in this world fashioned by māyā, abandon attachment to it, and move about freely.

In the thirty-second chapter an upward course through sāttvic dharmas is described, followed by return for one who lacks knowledge of reality. Having described the course of the sinful person, he now states in four verses the course of one who performs desire-motivated rites. A householder who remains at home milks his own dharmas for desire and wealth; he then again fills out and performs those very dharmas that he has milked for their fruits.
Even such a person, turned away from dharma in the form of worship of Bhagavān, worships the material deities and the ancestors.
His mind is pervaded by faith in those deities and ancestors, and his vows and observances are directed toward them. “Soma-drinkers” means that they drink Soma in that realm.
Having stated that one falls from the world of enjoyment when merit is exhausted, he now says that even those worlds themselves are dissolved at the daily pralaya.

In three verses he states that the very destination of those established in Bhagavān’s dharma is attainment of Him. They do not milk their own dharmas for the purposes of desire and wealth; they are unattached, and all their actions have been laid down and offered to the Lord.

They attain the all-faced, complete Puruṣa. Thus the śruti says that through the gate of the sun the stainless ones go where the immortal Puruṣa of imperishable nature is. “Prakṛti” is the material cause, while that which brings about origination and dissolution is the efficient cause.

In three verses beginning with the end of two parārdhas he states that worshippers of Hiraṇyagarbha who contemplate him with the vision of the Supreme Lord also attain the Supreme, but gradually. “Para” here means Hiraṇyagarbha, and “those who contemplate the Supreme” are those who worship Hiraṇyagarbha while seeing the Supreme Lord in him.

The cosmic egg is surrounded by the five great elements beginning with earth, by mind, the senses, their objects such as sound, and bhūtādi, ego. When the Lord wishes to withdraw that whole aggregate, He turns toward the unmanifest, and toward Time called “para,” whose measure is two parārdhas.

Those yogins who have gone far along that course and entered Bhagavān in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha attain together with him the immortal, supremely blissful Brahman; they do not attain it earlier. The smṛti likewise says that at the universal withdrawal all of them, together with Brahmā, enter the supreme state at the end of his term.
Worshippers of Bhagavān, however, attain Him directly, not by such a gradual path. Therefore, he says, you should worship Him directly, with bhāva—with love.

Thus it has been taught that devotees of Bhagavān attain Him directly and without interval, whereas worshippers of Hiraṇyagarbha who see him as non-different from Bhagavān attain Him gradually. But when Brahmā and others are worshipped as distinct, even they return—how much more so others. This is stated in four verses. Vedagarbha, Brahmā, when the guṇas are again disturbed, is born as before and again occupies the office of Brahmā; the construction is completed by the third verse. He is accompanied by the sages such as Marīci and by the great masters of yoga.

Two causes of such rebirth are stated: identification grounded in the perception of difference, and the sense of agency. The reason they return to their former positions is their karma; where that karma is without attachment and personal desire, it has the character described here.

What do they do before being born again here? First they enjoy the lordship of the highest cosmic office. Then, at dissolution, they reach the saguṇa Puruṣa, the first avatāra who presides over the guṇas. The sages and the others similarly enjoy the lordship produced by their own karma, reach the Puruṣa, and afterward return as before to their respective offices.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.

If even worshippers of Brahmā return in this way because of the perception of difference and the sense of agency, what need be said of performers of desire-motivated rites? Condemning them, he speaks in six verses. Those whose minds are attached to ritual action and who perform all the non-prohibited desire-motivated and obligatory acts go by the southern path of Aryaman, the path of smoke, to the world of the ancestors. The syntactic completion comes with the fifth verse; the intervening verses contain their censure.

Those devoted to the three worldly goals turn away from the stories of the slayer of Madhu, whose great deeds are worthy of narration and whose wisdom removes saṃsāra. Abandoning the nectar of Acyuta’s stories, they listen instead to the tales of the unholy. Such people, the verse says, have surely been assigned that course by fate.

From the world of the ancestors they are born again among their own descendants, such as their sons. They had performed the rites extending from conception through cremation; that is, they were performers of the prescribed ritual sequence.

additions.text: How are they born again? They fall back toward this world from the world of the ancestors when their rise—the means and power of enjoyment there—has been lost.
“Parameṣṭhin” here means the Supreme Lord. One should worship Him with one’s whole being, with exceedingly deep love, and with devotion that takes refuge in His qualities.
When He is worshipped, knowledge and detachment arise of themselves; this is the point of the verse beginning with Vāsudeva.

He establishes that point. When the devotee’s mind becomes steady in Bhagavān through loving attachment to His qualities, it no longer seizes upon the objects through the activities of the senses with a sense of inequality and difference.

At that very time he sees the self by the self as self-luminous. It is equal, and its vision is equal. Why? Because it is without attachment, for inequality arises from attachment. Its nonattachment is explained by its freedom from the distinction of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted. It has ascended and become firmly established in the state of conviction, “I am supreme bliss.”

He illustrates the sameness just stated. Pure knowledge alone is well known through expressions such as “the Supreme Brahman.” Through the categories of the seen, the seer, and the instrument of seeing it appears as though differentiated; in reality it is the same pure knowledge throughout.

An objection is raised: if pure knowledge is the very nature of the self and therefore eternally attained, why must it be attained through yoga produced by many disciplines? “Is joined or attained” is the sense: the fruit of yoga is simply the removal of association with the manifested world.

How can the manifested world, which is established by direct perception and the other means of knowledge, be removed? Because that perception is erroneous. For those whose awareness is turned outward, Brahman itself—pure knowledge and without guṇas—appears in the form of an object whose properties are sound and the rest; there is no separately existing object apart from that knowledge.

He illustrates this appearance in object-form. Ego is the form of “I” and is threefold, constituted of the three guṇas. It becomes fivefold again in the form of the elements and elevenfold in the form of the senses. “Svarāṭ” indicates the form of the living being. The living being’s body, the cosmic egg, and the world all appear from these principles beginning with mahat.
An objection is raised: if this is so, why does a person not apprehend it in this way? The verse answers by identifying this very reality as Brahman.
For easier comprehension he briefly repeats the meaning already taught. “O guervī” means “O venerable one.”

By this jñāna-yoga Bhagavān Himself is attained, just as by bhakti-yoga. Nirguṇa jñāna-yoga and the yoga characterized as devotion and fixed in Me have one and the same aim. That aim is the one indicated by the word “Bhagavān.” Thus the Gītā says, “They attain Me alone, delighting in the welfare of all beings.”

An objection is raised: scripture teaches that the fruit of jñāna-yoga is attainment of the self, while the fruit of bhakti-yoga is attainment of the Lord who is worshipped; how can their aim be one? He establishes this with an illustration. A single substance such as sugar or milk, the support of many qualities such as form and taste, is apprehended differently by senses proceeding along different paths: the eye apprehends it as white, the tongue as sweet, touch as cool, and so on. In the same way the one Bhagavān is known under these differing aspects.

He now elaborates the scriptural paths in three verses. “Kriyā” means meritorious works of the pūrta kind; “kratus” are sacrifices; “marśana” means Mīmāṃsā inquiry; and conquest of self and senses means abstention from what is prohibited.

“With both marks” means characterized by both desire-motivated and desireless performance. He identifies the one attained by them: even heaven and other results obtained through desire-motivated dharma are, in this sense, manifestations of Bhagavān’s own saguṇa form.
“By these paths” means by these several scriptural ways. “Sva-dṛk” means self-luminous.

Having thus concluded jñāna-yoga and stated that it has the same aim as bhakti-yoga, he summarizes bhakti-yoga and the rest in two verses beginning with “I have spoken.” It is fourfold through the divisions of the three guṇas and the nirguṇa form. “Antardhāvati” means that Time brings about origination, destruction, and the other transformations.
“Aṅga” here is a form of address: “O mother.”

In two verses beginning with “this should not be taught,” he indicates those who are not qualified for this teaching: one who causes distress or agitation to others, one who is divided and of bad conduct, and one who displays a banner of religion—that is, a hypocrite. The pinned source is terse in its first descriptive term, so the rendering follows the unambiguous qualifications without expanding it beyond the text.
In two verses beginning with “to one who has faith,” he states the qualifications of those to whom this teaching should be given.

He states that attainment of My path is also the fruit for one devoted to hearing and chanting this teaching. The word “and” has the force of “also”: that person too reaches My path; “hi” expresses certainty.

In the thirty-third chapter, through the instruction of that very Kapila, the liberation while living of His mother through knowledge is described. The veil and covering in the form of delusion had fallen from her. The tattvas themselves were the object of the accomplishment marked by Sāṅkhya knowledge, and this accomplishment became the ground and field from which her realization proceeded.

“Atha” introduces a new statement. Even the unborn Brahmā merely meditated on Your body; he did not directly behold it. Brahmā himself was born directly from the lotus of Your abdomen, and it is You who arrange the creation and the other functions of the universe—there is no one who creates You. How then could such a You have been borne within my womb? This is the connection of the three verses. The body is “sat,” manifest, because it lies within the cosmic waters. It is described as made of and pervaded by the elements, senses, their objects such as sound, and mind; this is because the stream of guṇas is present in it. Why so? Because it is the seed and cause of the entire aggregate of effects and causes.

How does such a Lord carry out creation and the rest? His power is divided and manifested as the flow of the guṇas. He performs these functions through His śakti, not by direct action, for He Himself is actionless. Why then does He cause creation even through śakti? Because His resolve is never false. For what purpose? He is the Lord of the living beings, and creation is for their field of experience. How can one Lord arrange innumerably diverse experiences? Because His powers are unthinkable and numberless.

Moreover, at dissolution this entire universe was within His belly; how then could He have been contained in my womb? If the answer is that He appeared as an infant, the verse recalls the infant upon the banyan leaf who drinks His own toe. This appearance as an infant is likewise His māyā.

Alternatively, You were not carried in my womb like an ordinary child; rather, like the Varāha and other avatāras, You manifested there solely by Your own will. “Deha-tantra” means that You accepted the apparatus of a body, a chosen form. The manifestation is for the subduing of the wicked, for the prosperity of those who obey Your command, and for making available the path of the self—the way of knowledge.

Therefore, by an argument from the greater to the lesser, she says that merely seeing Him has fulfilled her purpose. From hearing and repeating the name of the Lord, even a dog-eater becomes qualified for the Soma sacrifice. The statement indicates that such a person becomes worthy of honor.

She establishes the point in amazement. Even a dog-eater on whose tongue Your name is present is for that very reason most exalted. Why? Such persons have already performed austerity, offered oblations, bathed at holy places, become true Āryas of good conduct, and studied the Veda. The meaning may be that all these purifying acts are contained within chanting Your name; alternatively, the rise of the great fortune of chanting Your name reveals that they performed such acts in former births.

additions.text: “Pratyak-srotas” means the mind whose current has been drawn back inward toward the self; within such a mind He is to be fully contemplated. “He whose womb contains the Vedas” is the intended description.
She spoke with speech that was aviklava—steady, grave, and free from confusion.
By this teaching of Mine, which is easy to practice and which I have explained to you, and by actually undertaking it, you will reach the highest limit: liberation while living.
“Yāyāḥ” means “you will go.” “Those who do not know this” means those who are ignorant of My teaching and intention.
“Anumata” means permitted and given leave.

She became concentrated at Bindu-saras, which is like a floral crown upon the Sarasvatī. On the variant reading referring directly to the Sarasvatī, the lake is described as encircled by it like a crown.

He states the condition in which she became concentrated. By repeatedly immersing herself three times daily, she bore tawny-reddish locks that were naturally curling; she wore bark garments and her body had become lean.

She abandoned the household prosperity that had been greatly expanded through the austerity and yoga of Prajāpati Kardama. Distressed by separation from the Lord who had appeared as her son, she made her face indescribably overwhelmed by grief; the syntactic connection is completed later in the passage.
In that household were soft, white beds and coverings resembling milk foam, couches fashioned with ivory, furnishings made of gold, seats such as stools, and coverings pleasant to the touch.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
The place was beautiful with many celestial trees.
It was Devahūti herself who entered that garden.
She abandoned even that which was most intensely desired by the women of Indra, and abandoned her identification and attachment to it.
He shows how unbearable separation from a beloved can be: she became like a loving cow whose calf has been lost.
He now states the fruit of the meditation produced by separation. She became niḥspṛhā, entirely without worldly desire. “O child” is Maitreya’s address to Vidura.

Thereafter, meditating upon the form of Bhagavān exactly as her own son Kapila had taught, and meditating upon that very self as viśvato-mukha, all-pervading and facing everywhere, she became one whose mind was established in Brahman. With what did she meditate? With a purified self, that is, a purified mind. He states the causes of that purification: yoga in the form of an uninterrupted current of devotion, together with detachment, and knowledge produced by properly regulated practice. Proper regulation is what the Gītā describes: “For one regulated in food and recreation, regulated in exertion in actions, regulated in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.” This knowledge is a cause of Brahmanhood, bringing about establishment in Brahman. The reason the self is all-pervading is that through direct self-experience the delimitation produced by the guṇas of māyā has disappeared. The Brahman in which she is established is Bhagavān, the refuge of the living beings.

An objection is raised: if the guṇas still exist, how can there be no recollection of them? Because her samādhi had become permanently established and had gained firm footing. Through that state, the confusion caused by the guṇas had turned away and become quiet.

Her body was nourished by others, namely the Vidyādharī women created by Kardama. Because mental distress and dejection were absent, it did not become emaciated; though covered with bodily impurities, it still shone.
“Guarded by daiva” means sustained and protected by the portion of karma that had already begun to bear fruit.
The nirvāṇa spoken of here is described as eternal.
O heroic Vidura, “upeyuṣī” means that she attained and reached it.
O gentle one, that mortal body of hers became a river. Its mortal, bodily constituent impurities had been washed away and dissolved through yoga.
The statement that Kapila also departed is now elaborated in three verses. “Having obtained permission” means that He respectfully requested and received leave.
He was one to whom due honor, arghya, and a dwelling place were offered.
Worthy of the state of perfect tranquility, He remains established in concentration.
He concludes the subject under discussion with “this.” “Tava” means “by you.”
He states the fruit of hearing and chanting this account. “At Him whose banner bears Suparṇa” means at the Lord whose standard bears Garuḍa; such a person attains Him.
